title: The CIO’s Guide to Governing AI Agents
summary: A 28-point checklist for CIOs to score AI agent governance across ownership, identity, access, human review, evaluation and auditability.
body_markdown:
# Score Your AI Agent Governance in 28 Checks


The average Fortune 500 company is expected to run more than 150,000 AI agents by 2028. Only 13% of organizations say they have the governance to manage them, according to Gartner.


That gap tends to surface the hard way: an agent shares confidential data, or takes an action no one approved. This checklist finds it first. Work through six areas, tick a box only when the control is in place for every agent in production, and score yourself out of 28.


**Want the full guide?**[Download the CIO’s Guide to Governing AI Agents.](https://39942632.fs1.hubspotusercontent-na1.net/hubfs/39942632/Guide/StackAI_Agent_Governance_Checklist.pdf)


## Key Takeaways


-


Treat agents as non-human identities, with their own credentials, owners and lifecycle.


-


Give each agent only the access its job needs, for only as long as it needs it.


-


Require human approval before agents send, pay or write to a system of record.


-


Set a written accuracy target before launch, and monitor against it after.


-


Scored under 14? Pause new launches and start with ownership and access.


1.


## Give Every Agent an Owner and an Identity


An agent running on its builder's API keys is invisible to your identity team. The market is catching on: in October 2026, IBM announced a governed identity record per agent, short-lived least-privilege credentials, and one place to discover and contain them.


### Ownership (5 checks)


-


Each agent has a business owner and a technical owner on record.


-


Ownership transfers when someone changes roles or leaves.


-


Each agent has a written purpose: the one job it is approved to do.


-


There is a full inventory of agents in production, including ones built outside your main platform.


-


Retired agents are decommissioned, not left running.


### Identity (4 checks)


-


Each agent has its own entry in your identity system, such as Okta or Microsoft Entra, with its own credentials.


-


No agent runs on a shared or personal credential.


-


Lifecycle status (draft, testing, production, retired) is tracked per agent.


-


Each identity entry lists the owner, the job, and exactly what the agent can access or change.


1.


## Shrink Access to the Job


The most common failure isn't a rogue agent. It's an agent that can see more than the person asking it.


### Access Permissions (5 checks)


-


Each agent reaches only the data and systems its job requires.


-


Credentials are short-lived or rotated, never hardcoded in prompts or workflows.


-


Agents answer only from data the requesting user is already cleared to see.


-


Access can be revoked immediately.


-


The tools, MCP servers and integrations each agent can call are listed and approved.


1.


## Put People Before Consequential Actions


Agents can draft, check and recommend at scale. Sending, paying and writing to systems of record still need a human signature.


### Human Review Points (4 checks)


-


Consequential actions require human approval.


-


Low-confidence outputs are routed to a human reviewer.


-


Reviewers know what they are approving and can reject or edit.


-


Escalation paths are defined for exceptions the agent can't handle.


1.


## Test Before Launch, Trace Everything After


"It seemed to work in the demo" is not an accuracy target. Neither is a log nobody can read back.


### Evaluation (5 checks)


-


Each agent has a written accuracy target, such as 95% correct on real cases, and meets it before launch.


-


Test sets reflect real inputs, including edge cases and bad data.


-


Production accuracy is checked on a set cadence, with an alert if it drops.


-


Model and token costs are tracked per agent.


-


Changes to prompts, models or tools trigger re-testing.


### Auditability (5 checks)


-


Every run is logged: inputs, outputs, tools called and data sources used.


-


Answers cite their sources so reviewers can check them.


-


Writes to business systems carry provenance back to the agent run.


-


Approval decisions are recorded with who approved and when.


-


Logs are retained to match your regulatory requirements.


## What Your Score Tells You to Do


Add up your checks. Then find your weakest section. Start there, even if your total is high.


-


**0–13, ungoverned.** Agents are running ahead of controls. Pause new launches and start with ownership and access.


-


**14–22, partly governed.** Some controls exist, but not for every agent. Fix your weakest section before adding more.


-


**23–28, governed.** Controls are in place across all six areas. Expand to new teams and higher-risk workflows.


## Hold Vendors to the Same 28


A governed platform answers each of these with a feature you can see, not a roadmap slide. Ask to see it live, using one of your own workflows, like an IT support desk or KYC review.


-


**Ownership:** Can I see every agent in production, who owns it and what stage it's in?


-


**Identity:** Do agents and users sign in through our SSO, with roles we control?


-


**Access:** Can an agent ever return data the requesting user isn't cleared to see?


-


**Human review:** Where can I require approval before an agent acts, and who can approve?


-


**Evaluation:** How do I test an agent before launch and roll it out to a small group first?


-


**Auditability:** Can I trace a single answer back to every prompt, tool call and source behind it?

On StackAI, each checklist area maps to a control in the product: an agent development lifecycle with an owner at every stage, SSO and RBAC, permission-scoped answers across 500+ integrations, approval gates, feature-flagged rollouts, and traceability down to each tool call and prompt.
